The next most important factor was your class ranking in the third year of law school. This strong performance helped pull the prediction back toward passing.

Your LSAT score of 40 was the third most influential piece of information. While this is higher than the 37.18 average of accepted students, the model still interpreted it as contributing slightly toward a higher chance of failure.

In short, although you have solid credentials and performed very well in your later law school years, your undergraduate record weighed most heavily and tipped the scale just past the acceptance threshold.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider targeted bar-prep courses, especially those that address foundational legal reasoning that may connect to your earlier academic record. Retaking the LSAT could also help if you can raise it further. Many students in similar situations succeed on their second attempt after focused preparation.
